inline.s: [1. Do not store up wealth and property, build houses, buy fields and land, or acquire any exquisite fine things. Even sutras and images handed down from high antiquity, or produced by famous masters, cling to none of them; with one mind, right mindfulness.]

1. Do not accumulate wealth and property, build houses, buy fields and land, or procure any exquisite and fine objects. Even sutras and images handed down from high antiquity, though they come from famous masters, must not be clung to; with one mind, right mindfulness.

[One mind and right mindfulness] Master Lianchi says: "One who has set his mind on the study has but a single right thought, ever present in his breast. When he meets with stillness it is so; when he meets with clamor it is so. Let stillness and clamor come and go as they will — this thought of mine, this very one, is utterly unmoved. Only thus is there no interruption, and this is what is called skill in practice. Have you not heard the ancients say: the wise remove the mind, the foolish remove the environment? If one must shun the noisy and grasp at the still, then I fear there is no time when conditions are still, nor any place where they are still. As for seeking stillness, nothing surpasses the depths of the mountains. Yet the deep mountains are still — and there the woodcutter's axe is heard beyond the clouds, the cowherd's flute sounds in the slanting light: how then can the ear be still? The woodcutter's axe and the cowherd's flute might perhaps be shut out, so that they do not reach my ear; but when in the clear night the gibbon cries and the tiger roars, and in broad day the magpie chatters and the crow caws, how can one be still then? The gibbon's cry and the tiger's roar, the magpie's chatter and the crow's caw, might perhaps be driven away, so that they do not reach my ear; but when a wild wind rises and ten thousand hollows howl with rage, when a swift thunderbolt falls and a thousand mountains shake — at such a time, will the one who shuns clamor and grasps at silence shut them out? Drive them away? By this we may infer: there is surely no time when conditions are still, and surely no place where they are still. The student has only to fear that his resolve is not fierce! Keep one fierce resolve, and where can he not go?" (The Yunqi Dharma Collection)

[2. Do not undertake the various kinds of non-essential deeds of merit and affinity; wait until another day, when the great matter is already clear — then it will not be too late to do them. For now, set aside the gate of ten thousand practices; with one mind, right mindfulness.]

2. Do not undertake the various kinds of non-essential deeds of merit and affinity; for the time being, wait until another day when the great matter is already clear — it will not be too late to do them. For now, set aside the gate of ten thousand practices; with one mind, right mindfulness.

[The great matter] Here it means seeing the mind and seeing one's nature. For a reciter of the Buddha's name who has not yet attained one mind undisturbed, reciting the Buddha to the point of one mind undisturbed is the foremost great matter of ending birth and death. [The gate of ten thousand practices] "Ten thousand practices" means all practices. "Gate" carries the sense of entering and exiting. Chan Master Weishan Lingyou says: "In the ground of the true principle, not a mote of dust is admitted; within the gate of ten thousand practices, not a single dharma is abandoned." (The Sayings of Chan Master Weishan Lingyou of Tanzhou)

[3. Do not give rise to a mind of greed and love toward pleasing sights, pleasing tastes, and the like, nor toward those who praise me with kind words. Do not give rise to a mind of anger and affliction toward unpleasant sights, unpleasant tastes, and the like, nor toward those who revile me with harsh words, who abuse and insult me, who in all ways thwart me. Even things past and future, whether favorable or contrary, reject them all utterly; guard the firm rampart; with one mind, right mindfulness.]

3. Do not give rise to a mind of greed and love toward pleasing sights and delicious tastes and the like, nor toward those who praise me with kind words. Do not give rise to a mind of anger and affliction toward unpleasant sights and foul tastes and the like, nor toward those who revile me with harsh words, who abuse and insult me, who in all ways thwart me. Even things past and future, whether favorable or contrary, must all be
utterly cast off and cut away
, so that no mind of love and hate, of taking and rejecting, arises; guard the firm rampart; with one mind, right mindfulness.
[Firm rampart] A solid defensive wall.

[4. Do not compose poems and essays, do not write inscriptions, couplets, and matched scrolls in regular or cursive script, do not polish letters and correspondence, do not browse widely in outside books, do not discuss others' merits and faults, strengths and weaknesses — still less teach from personal conjecture and write loftily of one's own views, or, while Chan is not yet thoroughly awakened, presume to pick out the ancients and comment on them. Seal the mouth and tie the tongue; with one mind, right mindfulness.]

4. Do not chant poems or write essays, do not write inscriptions, couplets, and matched scrolls in regular script (zhenshu) or cursive script, do not polish letters and correspondence (chidu), or leaf through outside books. Do not discuss others' merits and faults, strengths and weaknesses; still less, relying merely on one's own private views, write loftily and self-importantly (gaoxin). If one's Chan practice is not yet thoroughly awakened, one must not presume to pick out ancient cases and comment on them. One should seal the mouth and tie the tongue; with one mind, right mindfulness.

[Polishing letters and correspondence] Revising and embellishing the wording of letters so as to make them perfect. [Outside books] The Buddha's teaching texts are inner texts; all books besides these are called outside books. [Personal conjecture] One's own private views. [Picking and commenting] Picking out the ancients and commenting on them. "Picking out the ancients" means taking up ancient cases and koans to awaken students of Chan; "commenting on them" means evaluating and advocating the sayings of the ancients.
[5. Do not form ties with relatives and friends, do not accept invitations and summonses, do not wander the mountains and enjoy the scenery, do not indulge in miscellaneous idle
(the source's jian is a graphic variant of xian)
talk. Of all the various matters within worldly truth, except those that ought by principle to be done and can in no way be set aside, put all the rest to rest; with one mind, right mindfulness.]

5. Do not form ties with relatives and friends, take part in social obligations such as invitations and summonses, wander the mountains and enjoy the scenery, or engage in miscellaneous idle talk. Of all the various worldly matters, except those that ought by principle to be done and can in no way be declined, dispense with all the rest; with one mind, right mindfulness.
[6. Do not cling and give way to heedlessness, do not indulge and give free rein to sleep. While the great matter is not yet clear, bear toil and endure hardship; with one mind, right mindfulness.]

6. Do not cling, do not let body and mind run loose, do not give free rein to sleep. While the great matter is not yet clear, one must toil diligently and endure hardship; with one mind, right mindfulness.

[7. Do not vie with worldly people in talent and ability, contend for fame and power, claim to have attained what you have not attained, claim to have realized what you have not realized, falsely style yourself a good teacher, or vainly exalt yourself. You should only hold to humility and keep to simplicity, dwell all your life on the ground of a learner, temper yourself, and ever advance with diligence; with one mind, right mindfulness.]

7. Do not compete with worldly people in talent, contend for fame and power, claim to have attained what you have not attained, claim to have realized what you have not realized, falsely call yourself a good teacher, or vainly exalt yourself. One should only hold to humility and keep to simplicity, dwell all one's life on the ground of a learner, temper oneself, and advance without cease; with one mind, right mindfulness.

[Claiming to have attained what one has not attained, claiming to have realized what one has not realized] To say that one has already obtained the noble dharmas when one has not, and to say one has already realized the fruit of the Way when one has not.

In the Qing dynasty there was an old woman known as "Care-About-Nothing"; we do not know her name, and know only that she was a native of Hangzhou. She once asked the monk Daoyuan of the Xiaoci Nunnery, "What dharma-gate should one cultivate to be certain of escaping the sea of suffering in this lifetime?" The monk Daoyuan answered, "Nothing surpasses reciting the Buddha's name. Yet reciting the Buddha's name is not hard; the difficulty lies in
lasting long
; lasting long is not hard — the difficulty lies in
single-mindedness

. If you can set aside all worldly affairs and single-mindedly uphold the Name and recite the Buddha, with sincere resolve to seek rebirth, then at death the Buddha will come to receive you, and you will escape the sea of suffering!" The old lady joyfully bowed in thanks. When she returned home she at once entrusted the household affairs to her daughters-in-law, set apart a pure chamber where she enshrined a Buddha image, and practiced within it.

After more than a year had passed, she came again to ask the monk Daoyuan: "Ever since receiving your instruction, your disciple has given up household affairs and applies herself with a single mind to reciting the Buddha's name. I can say of myself that I have been able to recite long without slackening, but I am tormented by the difficulty of single-mindedness and cannot attain it. Pray, master, teach me once more what to do." The monk Daoyuan said, "Although you have cast off the household affairs, you are still not without attachment to your sons, grandsons, and relatives. If this root of love is not pulled up, how can you attain single-mindedness? To advance a step further, you must first pull up the root of love, put down everything, and only then can you attain single-mindedness!" The old lady sighed, "How right the master is! Though my body no longer concerns itself, my mind has still not let go. From today on I truly will become a person who cares about nothing!" From then on she practiced all the more earnestly. When the thought of love stirred now and then, she would at once silently recite the three words "care about nothing" to drive it off. When she was asked about household affairs, she likewise refused with these three words. Thus the great name "Care-About-Nothing" spread among her relatives and through the village. In this way more than another year passed. One day she came to the Xiaoci Nunnery, bowed in thanks to Daoyuan, and said, "The master has not deceived me; your disciple is to travel West within a few days!" Several days later, she passed away without any illness.

Original text: In the Qing dynasty, an old woman called Care-About-Nothing, whose surname is lost, was a native of Hangzhou. Once she asked the monk Daoyuan of Xiaoci Nunnery, "What dharma-gate should one cultivate to be certain of leaving the sea of suffering in this lifetime?" The monk said, "None surpasses reciting the Buddha's name. Yet reciting the name is not hard; what is hard is lasting long. Lasting long is not hard; what is hard is single-mindedness. If you can disregard everything, set your mind singly on upholding the Name, and with complete sincerity resolve to seek rebirth, then at death the Buddha will come to receive you and you will escape the sea of suffering." Joyfully she bowed in thanks. At once she entrusted her household affairs to her daughters-in-law and the like, set apart a pure chamber to enshrine the Buddha, and practiced within it. After more than a year she went again to ask him, saying, "Ever since receiving your instruction, your disciple has set aside household affairs and confined herself to reciting the Buddha's name. Of myself I can say that I have been able to recite long without slackening, but I am tormented by the difficulty of single-mindedness; the master must have something to teach me!" The monk said, "Though you have cast off household affairs, you are not without attachment to your sons, grandsons, and relations. This is the root of love not yet drawn out; how can you attain single-mindedness? Now make further effort, first drawing out the root of love and putting down everything; only then can you attain single-mindedness." Sighing, she said, "The master's words are right. Though I no longer concern my body, I cannot help but concern my mind; from today on I truly remain one who cares about nothing." So she pressed on all the more earnestly. When the thought of love stirred now and then, she silently held to the three words "care about nothing" to drive it away. When she was consulted about household affairs, she likewise refused with these three words. Thus the name Care-About-Nothing spread among her relations and friends. After another year she went to the nunnery to thank him, saying, "The master does not deceive me; your disciple's day to travel West is set." A few days later, she died without any illness. (Recorded from the Essentials of Buddha-Recitation.)

On New Year's Eve of the yichou year of the Jiajing reign (1565), Master Lianchi asked his wife, Lady Tang, to brew tea. As Lady Tang carried the tea to the desk, it slipped from her hands and fell to the floor. Seeing the beloved heirloom jade cup shattered, the Master smiled and said:
"All causes and conditions must eventually disperse."

The next year, he bade Lady Tang farewell, saying: "Affection cannot last forever, and in birth and death no one can take another's place. I am going to leave home; make good arrangements for yourself." Lady Tang, likewise free and easy, said: "You go first; once I have arranged the household, I too shall leave home." Thereupon the Master composed the verses "Canceled in One Stroke" and left home.

[Canceled in one stroke] This is an old phrase from settling accounts, meaning to wipe out a debt that has been repaid with one stroke of the brush; later it was extended to mean canceling everything entirely. For example, the late-Tang Daoist Lü Dongbin, in his awakening lyric "Qinyuan Chun," wrote: "Enough, enough — turn back early, and wipe away the romantic past with one stroke."

"Parental kindness is heavy as hills and peaks; offerings of five cauldrons and three beasts cannot repay its due. When one's parents leave the dust and grime, the child's duty is then complete. Cha! The great cause of leaving home — how can worldly feeling fathom it through? Filial sons and worthy grandsons should investigate true emptiness; therefore the five-colored golden insignia are canceled in one stroke."

Parents' kindness is weighty as hills and peaks; the five cauldrons and three beasts are not enough to repay it. One must surely rescue both parents from birth and death before the child's filial duty is complete. Cha! The great cause of leaving home — how could the understanding of ordinary beings see through it? Truly filial sons and worthy grandsons should investigate the true reality of all dharmas (only by attaining the Way oneself can one rescue one's parents from the sea of birth and death); therefore the five-colored golden insignia of honor to one's parents and glory to one's ancestors are canceled in one stroke.

[Five cauldrons and three beasts] A description of extremely lavish offerings. [Five cauldrons] In ancient sacrificial rites, a grandee used five cauldrons. [Three beasts] Ox, sheep, and pig. [When one's parents leave the dust and grime, the child's duty is then complete] This means: when one's parents have ended birth and death (left the dust and grime), only then have the children truly fulfilled their filial duty. [Cha
chā

] An exclamation; here it is a blow to the head (a sudden shout of awakening). [True emptiness] The true reality of all dharmas. [The true reality of all dharmas] The actual state of all things. The Buddha Repository Sutra says:
"What is called the true reality of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty and without anything there is."
(For details, see
The True Reality of All Dharmas
[Five-colored golden insignia] The official robes of high officials in ancient times; here it refers to attaining success and fame, honoring one's parents, and bringing glory to one's ancestors.
Master Hanshan said:

"What parents throughout the world hope for in their children is that they attain fame and honor their parents; thus they regard the support of the three beasts and five cauldrons as fulfilling filial piety. Little do they know that the richer the support, the deeper the suffering; this burdens one's parents and is not true filial piety. Thus our Buddha, the World-Honored One, regarded the golden wheel
(scorned the position of the wheel-turning king)

as worthless, left his parents, abandoned the royal palace, practiced austerities in the snowy mountains, and in six years attained the Way, becoming honored in the three realms and revered by humans and gods. Had he not cast aside the most precious things and cut off great love, how could he have won the imperishable work of long kalpas? Hence it is said: 'The greatly filial Śākya, the World-Honored One, repaid his parents' kindness across kalpas.' Is this not taking the realization of the unborn and the universal deliverance of living beings as the ground of repaying them? The Buddha taught the great precepts, beginning with: filial piety is called the precept. That is, to be filial to one's parents, filial to one's teachers and the monastic order and the Three Jewels, filial to the supreme Way, and filial to all living beings. Therefore, one who truly studies and practices the Buddha's path will regard all living beings as one's parents of many lives — how could one not repay the parents of this one life
(how could one fail to repay the kindness of this life's parents)
(The Dream Journey Collection
, "Instructing Layman Wang Zi'an on Sending His Son to Leave Home")

blocks.text: 2. The Chapter on Husband and Wife

inline.s: "Phoenix mates and paired lovebirds, when will the tangle of affection ever end? Living ghosts keep each other company in disguise, and when the affinity ends they still part. Cha! For your two hearts entwined, you wear the cangue and carry the shackles. See through the enemy — each seeks a gate of escape; therefore the fish-and-water couple is canceled in one stroke."

Phoenix mates and paired lovebirds — when will the tangle of affection ever end? Are you not just a pair of living ghosts keeping each other company in disguise, parting when the affinity ends? Cha! For your two hearts' tender entanglement, you wear the cangue and drag the shackles. See through the enemy who comes to collect the debt — each seeks a gate of liberation and walks away; therefore the fish-and-water couple is canceled in one stroke.
[Phoenix mates and paired lovebirds] Refers to the intimacy of man and woman, harmonious companions like phoenix and lovebird. [Shackles
chǒu
] A kind of ancient manacle. [Entwined
chóu móu

] Deep, tender, lingering affection: two hearts entwined. [Enemy] A foe who has come for revenge. "Husband and wife are enemies" means that each drags the other down, suffering endlessly in the cycle of birth and death. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
"You love my mind, I cherish your form; by this cause and condition, through a hundred thousand kalpas, we remain ever entangled."

The way to resolve it is to enter the gate of liberation, turning lovers into companions on the Way. [Each seeks a gate of escape] Each seeks the gate for ending birth and death (the Buddha's gate) and walks through it.

blocks.text: 3. The Chapter on Children and Grandchildren

inline.s: "The body is like a sore and a wen
(yóu)

; do not make distant worries for your children and grandchildren. Recall the Dou of Mount Yan — does he still remain today? Cha! After all there comes an end; all returns to nothing after. Who recognizes the person himself, unchanging as of old for myriad ages? Therefore the fine sons and grandsons are canceled in one stroke."

The physical body is filthy and painful like a sore or a wen; do not make distant worries for your children and grandchildren. Recall the Dou of Mount Yan, who taught his five sons and made their names known throughout the land — do they still remain today? Cha! After all there comes an end; all returns to nothing after; on the road to the yellow springs one walks alone. Who recognizes the person himself (the self-nature), unchanging as of old for myriad ages (never aging and never dying)? Therefore the fine sons and grandsons are canceled in one stroke.

[The Dou of Mount Yan] This is Dou Yujun, of the Later Jin period of the Five Dynasties. His native home was Yuyang in Jizhou, in the region of Mount Yan, so later generations respectfully called him Dou Yanshan — the old custom of using a place name in place of a personal name as a mark of respect. He was strict in family discipline and had five sons, all of whom excelled in both learning and conduct; people of the time praised them as the "Five Dragons of the Dou family." All passed the jinshi examination and became pillars of the state. The Three Character Classic says: "Dou Yanshan, with right methods, taught his five sons, all of whom made their names known." [Do they still remain today] "Where are the generals and ministers of old and new? A mound of wild grass covers all that's left." [All returns to nothing after] When the last breath fails to come, one walks the yellow springs alone; ultimately speaking, what descendants or heirs are there at all? [Who recognizes the person himself] Who realizes that the self-nature alone is truly oneself? Living beings are deluded, falsely taking the physical body for the self, and do not realize that the self-nature is who they really are; hence there is the cycle of birth and death. The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
"All living beings, from time without beginning, are variously inverted, like a person who has lost his way and mistakes the four directions
(for example, taking east for west and south for north)

, falsely taking the four great elements for the appearance of the self and the shadows of the six sense-objects for the appearance of their own mind. It is like diseased eyes that see flowers in the sky and a second moon. ...... From this false existence they revolve in birth and death; hence it is called ignorance."

[The four great elements] The great element of earth, the great element of water, the great element of fire, and the great element of wind. Earth has solidity as its nature, water has moisture as its nature, fire has warmth as its nature, and wind has movement as its nature. All material things in the world possess the four natures of solidity, moisture, warmth, and movement, and so are called "great elements." The physical body is composed of the four great elements; here "the four great elements" refers to the physical body. [The shadows of the six sense-objects] The various thoughts produced when the six sense-roots engage the six sense-objects; since these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadows of the six sense-objects — the illusory shadows of the six sense-objects. [Fine sons and grandsons] A term of praise for a person's descendants. When children and grandchildren are simultaneously distinguished and flourishing, it is called "orchid and cassia blooming together."

blocks.text: 4. The Chapter on Fame and Achievement

inline.s: "Standing alone atop the turtle's head, say not this is a man's season of triumph. The golden seal hangs like a dipper, its show of power cannot last long. Cha! How much striving in vain, from a boy's face to hoary head. When the dream of yellow millet ends, one smiles at the nothingness; therefore wealth, rank, and renown are canceled in one stroke."

Standing alone atop the turtle's head — say not this is a man's season of triumph. The golden seal hangs like a dipper, but its show of power cannot last long. Cha! How much striving in vain, as a boy's face turns in a blink to a hoary head. When the dream of yellow millet wakes, look and see what remains; therefore wealth, rank, and renown are canceled in one stroke.

[Standing alone atop the turtle's head] "The turtle's head" is the relief carving of a giant turtle on the steps before the palace gate. When the list of successful jinshi candidates was posted, the top candidate (zhuangyuan) stood upon it to receive the announcement. [How much striving in vain] "Where are the generals and ministers of old and new? A mound of wild grass covers all that's left." (The Song of the Good End, from The Dream of the Red Chamber.) [The dream of yellow millet] An allusion from the Tang dynasty Record Within the Pillow: "In the seventh year of the Kaicheng reign, there was a student of the Lu family, named Ying, styled Cuizhi. At an inn in Handan (an inn), he met the Daoist Old Man Lü. The student sighed deeply over his poverty and hardship, and the old man took a pillow from his bag and gave it to him, saying: 'Pillow your head on this pillow of mine, and I shall make you honored, distinguished, and content!' At that moment the innkeeper was just steaming millet (yellow millet), and the student lowered his head onto the pillow and fell into a dream within it. He returned to his home, and within a few months married a daughter of the Cui family of Qinghe. The wife was exceedingly beautiful, and the dowry (marriage portion) grew ever richer, and the student was overjoyed. Then, soon (before long), he passed the jinshi examination and rose through the offices to be a secretariat drafter (accumulating merit and rising to be a drafter of the Central Secretariat), and was transferred to be a military governor (promoted to military governor), and routed the barbarians, becoming chancellor (serving as chancellor) for more than ten years. His five sons all held office (became officials), and his ten-odd grandsons, through their marriages (in-laws), were all connected with the most eminent families of the realm (illustrious clans), and he died at over eighty (zú: passed away). When he awoke, the millet was not yet cooked. Astonished (amazed), he said: 'Could it have been a dream (could this be a dream)?' The old man laughed and said: 'The fortunes of a man's life (circumstances) are just like this!' The student stood dazed (at a loss) for a long while, then bowed deeply in thanks and left." [Yellow millet] Yellow grain. [Bow deeply] To kneel, cup one's hands to the ground, and lower the head to the ground.

"Richer than princes and lords — you call it joy, I call it sorrow. The seeker endures much hardship; the gainer fears ruin. Cha! Plain rice surpasses rare delicacies, patched robes are like embroidery. Heaven and earth are my cottage — what need to build great mansions? Therefore house, land, and garden are canceled in one stroke."

Richer than princes and lords — you say I am joyful, I say it is sorrow: in seeking it, one endures a thousand hardships; having gained it, one fears ruin. Cha! Coarse tea and plain rice surpass rare delicacies; patched robes and worn jackets are like embroidered brocade. Heaven and earth are my house — what need to build great mansions? Therefore house, land, and garden are canceled in one stroke.

[You call it joy, I call it sorrow] You think that because I am richer than princes and lords I must be greatly delighted, not knowing the bitterness within: in pursuit of wealth I endured a thousand hardships; and if by luck I grew rich, I am ever anxious that officials, thieves, flood, fire, or a prodigal son may ruin my wealth. [Endure] To suffer; to toil.

blocks.text: 6. The Chapter on Talent and Learning

inline.s: "The sea of learning flows forever; the array of letters shines up to the Dipper and the Herd-boy star. One roams amid the hundred arts, and at a gallon of wine, a thousand poems. Cha! Brocade fills your breast — why boast? Before birth and death, it cannot save you in the least; therefore world-surpassing writing is canceled in one stroke."

The sea of learning flows without rest; the literary arena's radiance shines to the Dipper and the Herd-boy; one roams at will amid the hundred arts, and at a gallon of wine, a thousand poems. Cha! Brocade fills your breast — why boast? Before birth and death, not a thread of it can save you; therefore world-surpassing writing is canceled in one stroke.
[The sea of learning] In the Han dynasty, Yang Xiong's Model Sayings

, "Learning and Conduct," it says: "The hundred rivers, learning from the sea, reach the sea; the hills, learning from the mountain, do not reach the mountain." This means: the hundred rivers flow without ceasing, and so reach the sea; the hills stand still and do not move, and so do not reach the mountain. Therefore, in pursuing learning one should be like rivers flowing toward the sea, advancing day by day without cease. [The array of letters] The literary arena.
[The array of letters shines up to the Dipper and the Herd-boy star] A description of the height of a person's talent and learning: in the literary arena his radiance is boundless
, shining up to the Dipper (the Northern Dipper) and the Herd-boy star (the Altair star).

blocks.text: 7. The Chapter on Pleasure and Amusement

inline.s: "Summer outings and spring excursions, pleasures crowd the halls of song and dance; mist and rain blur the flowers and willows, chess and wine delight kin and friends. Cha! Before your eyes you flaunt your charm, but the suffering returns after death. What a pity to waste the light, ashamed and empty when you turn to look back; therefore the feelings of romance are canceled in one stroke."

Summer outings and spring excursions, pleasures crowd the halls of song and dance; mist and rain blur the flowers and willows, tea, wine, qin, and chess delight kin and friends. Cha! Before their eyes each one flaunts his charm, but the suffering returns to oneself after death. What a pity to waste the light and miss the great matter of birth and death; in shame and regret one turns to look back in vain; therefore the feelings of romance are canceled in one stroke.

[Before one's eyes] At present, now, the present time. [Charm (fengliu)] Having both achievement and literary refinement. [Ashamed (mǒ luó)] Sanskrit, translated as "ashamed." [Turn to look back in vain] Looking back on past affairs, all is emptiness.

Time passes swiftly and human life is impermanent. Students of the Buddha must be alert at all times, and by no means take it lightly, indulging in play and amusement and squandering the time, only to regret it endlessly. Samantabhadra Bodhisattva's Verse Admonishing the Assembly says:
"This day is already past, and life decreases with it, like a fish in dwindling water. What joy is there in
(this)
? O great assembly! Strive diligently, as if saving your head from burning! Only be mindful of impermanence
(think at every moment of the coming of death)
, and never be heedless
(by no means let yourself go, indulging in ease and pleasure and wasting this precious time)
[A fish in dwindling water] A fish in a pond whose water dries up day by day.
[Strive diligently, as if saving your head from burning]
A great fire is blazing on your head, and death draws swiftly near; in reciting the Buddha's name one should be
diligent and unremitting,
swiftly
impatiently extinguish this fire of death, and before unconsciousness and death overtake one, accomplish "the ten recitations in continuity, until habit becomes nature" (see
The Conditions for Rebirth

for details). [Impermanence] Not abiding forever (all dharmas of the world arise and cease in flux, not staying for an instant); also refers to death, the ghost that seizes the soul. [Be not heedless] By no means let yourself go, craving ease and comfort and wasting this precious time. The Buddha said:
"Though one toils for a lifetime, in but an instant afterward one is reborn in the Land of Measureless Life, with joy without limit."
(The Buddha Speaks the Sūtra of the Buddha of Measureless Life)
Truly:
In life one exhausts a thousand schemes of mind; after death, one leaves but a pair of empty hands behind.
Sorrow and joy, parting and meeting, clamor day after day; long life and early death, want and success, busy each and every day.
Cease to contend for strength and vie for victory; a hundred years is naught but a theater of play.
The moment the gongs and drums fall still, one knows not where the final exit may be.

blocks.text: Chapter 10: Right Mindfulness at the Time of Death

inline.s: For one who recites the Buddha's name, single-minded right mindfulness at the time of death is of the utmost importance. The thousands upon thousands of recitations, and even reciting all day and all year, are nothing but the ripening of this one thought of Buddha-recitation, so as to ensure that at the time of death this thought continues uninterrupted and evokes Amitabha Buddha to appear before one and receive one. Master Lianchi taught: "Now that one is single-mindedly undefiled, within, right mindfulness congeals; without, the Buddha's welcome is evoked; casting off this karmic body, one is reborn in that land." (Commentary on the Amitabha Sutra)
The patriarchs' relevant teachings are now transcribed with annotations as follows.
The following teaching is recorded from
Master Shandao's Essay on Right Mindfulness for Rebirth at Death

[If, when the illness is grave and death approaches, relatives must not shed tears and weep, nor utter sounds of sighing and grief, confusing the sick person's mind and spirit and causing him to lose right mindfulness. Rather, they should recite the Buddha's name aloud together, and only after the breath has ceased may they wail and weep. The moment there is the slightest attachment to the world, it becomes a hindrance and one cannot be liberated. If one can have someone who understands the Pure Land come frequently to encourage him, that is extremely fortunate. If one acts accordingly, one will certainly be reborn in transcendence — of this there is no doubt.]

If, when the illness is grave and death approaches, the relatives must not shed tears and weep, nor utter sounds of sighing and grief, lest the sick person's mind and spirit be confused and he lose right mindfulness. Rather, they must recite the Buddha's name in unison, and only after the sick person's breath has ceased may they wail and weep. For the moment the sick person has the slightest attachment to the world, it becomes a hindrance to rebirth and he cannot be liberated. If one can have someone who understands the Pure Land come frequently to encourage him, this is most fortunate. If one acts accordingly, the sick person will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, beyond all doubt.

Whether cleric or layperson, or one who has never recited the Buddha's name, whoever uses this method will be reborn — of this there is no doubt. I have often seen people who in ordinary times recite the Buddha's name, bow, and praise, and vow to be reborn in the West, with great earnestness
(sincere and zealous)

Yet when illness comes, they fear death and say nothing at all about rebirth and liberation. Only when breath has ceased and life is over, and consciousness has fallen into the dark realm, do they begin the ten recitations. This is like shutting the gate after the thief has gone — what use is it? The matter of birth and death is grave, and one must apply one's own effort to succeed
. If a single thought goes astray, one suffers for kalpas on end — who will take one's place? Think on this! Think on this!
When there is nothing the matter, one should take up this method diligently and uphold it; this is the great matter of the time of death.]

This method of "right mindfulness for rebirth at death" (the sick person must strive to maintain right mindfulness at death; relatives must not weep and wail, lest they disturb the sick person's right mindfulness at death; and a good teacher's constant guidance and encouragement can help the sick person raise up and maintain right mindfulness at death) — whether cleric or layperson, or one who has never recited the Buddha's name, whoever uses it will be reborn, beyond all doubt. I have seen many people in the world who in ordinary times recite the Buddha's name, bow, and praise, and vow to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss with great sincerity and zeal. Yet when illness comes, they fear death and say nothing at all about rebirth and liberation. Only when their own breath has ceased and life is over, and their consciousness has fallen into the dark realm, do they begin the ten recitations. This is like shutting the gate after the thief has gone (the thief has already carried the goods away, and only then does one shut the gate to guard against theft) — what use is it? The matter of birth and death is grave, and one must diligently apply one's own effort. If the single thought at death goes astray, the consequence is suffering for kalpas on end — who will take one's place? You must consider this well! Consider it well! Before illness has yet come, one should diligently take up and uphold this method of "right mindfulness for rebirth at death" (one must make full preparation for right mindfulness at death — this is what Master Yongming called "preparing the ford and bridge in advance" — and one should also warn one's relatives that they must not weep and wail at that time; it would be even better to have the help of a good teacher at death). This is the great matter of the time of death!
Master Lianchi's Commentary on the Amitabha Sutra says:

[Those who are confused at the end of life are so because in ordinary times they follow delusive thoughts, do not cultivate right mindfulness, and their minds are mostly scattered. When the warmth of the body is about to be relinquished, all that they have done in their lives appears before them, and their minds and spirits are terrified, their movements and pauses wild and flustered. Those who should enter hell see mountains of knives and forests of swords as pleasure gardens. Those who should fall among animals take the womb of a horse or the belly of a donkey as a splendid hall. Even those who have done good and should be born as humans or gods cannot avoid feeling love and hatred toward their parents. Even the small saints of initial resolve cannot correctly know their entering and departing. All of this is what is called confusion. Riding on this confusion, they receive rebirth according to karma within the three realms and seven destinies. Now, since one is single-mindedly undefiled,
within, right mindfulness congeals; without, the Buddha's welcome is evoked

, and casting off this karmic body, one is born in that land. As the Buddha said, "When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure," and again, "All Buddha-lands are upheld by thought alone." When the pure contemplation is accomplished, one will certainly attain rebirth — of this there is no doubt.]

Those who are confused at the end of life are all so because in ordinary times they follow delusive thoughts, do not cultivate right mindfulness, and their minds are mostly scattered. When the four elements dissolve, all that they have done in their lives appears before them, and their minds and spirits are terrified and their bearing loses all composure. Those who should enter hell see mountains of knives and forests of swords as beautiful gardens. Those who should fall among animals take the womb of a horse or the belly of a donkey for a magnificent hall. Even those who have done good and should be born in the human or heavenly realm cannot avoid, at the moment of entering the womb, loving the mother and hating the father and so taking a male body, or loving the father and hating the mother and so taking a female body. Even the small saints of the first fruit and bodhisattvas of initial resolve still have the delusion of the intervening skandha and cannot correctly know their entering and departing from the womb. All of this is confusion. Because of this confusion at the end of life, they receive rebirth according to karma within the seven destinies of the three realms. Now that one has accomplished single-mindedness in reciting the Buddha's name, then at the end of life, within, right mindfulness congeals, and without, the Buddha's welcome is evoked; casting off this karmic body, one goes directly to rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Just as the Buddha said: 'When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.' (When one's mind is pure, the Buddha-land in which one is born is also pure.) The Buddha also said: 'All Buddha-lands are upheld by thought alone.' (All Buddha-lands are entirely upheld by the mind's thought.) Therefore, when one who recites the Buddha's name accomplishes the pure contemplation, one will certainly attain rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Of this, of course, there is not the slightest doubt.

[The seven destinies] Hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, immortals, gods, and asuras. "Destiny" means the direction toward which one tends. [Buddha-land] The territory taught and transformed by one Buddha; there are distinctions of pure land, defiled land, reward land, and dharma-nature land.
Master Ouyi's Essential Explanation of the Buddha-Spoken Amitabha Sutra says:

[Q: Does reciting the name with a scattered mind also remove offenses? A: The merit of the name is inconceivable — how could it fail to remove offenses? But it does not ensure rebirth, because leisurely, scattered goodness is hard pressed to match the offenses accumulated since beginningless time. You should know that if the accumulated offenses had substance and form, the entire realm of empty space could not contain them; though for a hundred years, day and night, one recite Amitabha a hundred thousand times, and each utterance erases offenses of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death, still the offenses erased are like soil on the fingernail, while the offenses not erased are like the soil of the great earth. Only when one recites to the point of single-mindedness is it like a strong man breaking out through a siege, no longer to be held back by the three armies.]

Q: Does reciting the Buddha's name with a scattered mind also remove offenses? A: The merit of the name is inconceivable — how could it fail to remove offenses? But it does not necessarily lead to rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is because leisurely, scattered goodness is hard pressed to match the offenses accumulated since beginningless time. One should know that if the offenses accumulated since beginningless time had substance and form, the entire realm of empty space could not contain them; though in a hundred years one recites Amitabha a hundred thousand times each day and night, and each utterance erases eighty billion kalpas of grave offenses of birth and death, still the offenses erased are like soil on the fingernail, while the offenses not erased are like the soil of the ten directions' great earth. Only when one recites to the point of single-mindedness is it like a warrior breaking out through a siege, and the three armies of the foe (that is, afflictions and karmic obstacles) can do nothing to him.

Here Master Ouyi clearly points out that reciting the Buddha's name with a scattered mind is not incapable of removing offenses, but does not necessarily lead to rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and he explains the principle: "You should know that if the accumulated offenses had substance and form, the entire realm of empty space could not contain them; though for a hundred years, day and night, one recite Amitabha a hundred thousand times, and each utterance erases offenses of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death, still the offenses erased are like soil on the fingernail, while the offenses not erased are like the soil of the great earth." Then what should one do? Master Ouyi continues: "Only when one recites to the point of single-mindedness is it like a strong man breaking out through a siege, no longer to be held back by the three armies." Therefore the way out is "only reciting to the point of single-mindedness." This is why the World-Honored One clearly taught that one should recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly, and repeatedly urged one to "practice as taught."

[Soil on the fingernail] Also written "soil on the nail"; soil on a fingernail. In the scriptures and treatises, soil on the fingernail is often compared with the soil of the great earth as a simile, describing the former as extremely small and the latter as extremely abundant.
